summary: Describes Time To Live handling in hierarchical MPLS networks, formalizing a TTL-transparent mode for a label-switched path. It specifies the Pipe and Uniform models for tunnels, with examples of pushing and popping labels, and updates RFC 3032.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3443 defines how MPLS routers update the packet's time-to-live value as labels are added, swapped or removed. The Uniform model counts the tunnel's routers, while the Pipe models hide the tunnel interior from the tunneled packet's count.

subtitle: How MPLS tunnels count packet hops under the Uniform, Pipe and Short Pipe models.

tldr.problem: Earlier MPLS rules did not define TTL handling for hierarchical tunnels, Pipe models or Penultimate Hop Popping.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how routers choose an incoming TTL, decrement it and set outgoing IP or label TTLs for Uniform, Pipe and Short Pipe LSPs.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure whether tunnel routers are visible in the TTL count. RFC 3443 updates RFC 3032 and was later updated by RFC 5462.

facts.label: Tunneled TTL decrease in Pipe model

today: RFC 3443 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003. It updates RFC 3032 and was later updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: Why MPLS TTL Rules Needed Expansion
sections.content:
An MPLS label carries a Time To Live (TTL) value so packets cannot circulate indefinitely. RFC 3032 covered the Uniform model but did not specify hierarchical LSPs, the Pipe and Short Pipe models, or TTL handling with Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP).

RFC 3443 defines those cases and updates RFC 3032. It also states that choosing an LSP model is outside its scope and is configured by a network operator.
sections.plainLanguage: The MPLS hop counter needs rules for tunnels that can contain other paths. This RFC defines those rules for three tunnel models.

sections.title: Incoming and Outgoing TTL
sections.content:
The RFC calls the value used as the incoming TTL iTTL. The outgoing TTL, oTTL, is usually iTTL minus one. A router checks whether oTTL is greater than zero; if the check fails, the packet is not forwarded.

For an arriving IP packet, iTTL is the IP TTL. For an MPLS packet being pushed, swapped or PHP-popped, iTTL comes from the top incoming label. When a router pops a tunnel label, the selected iTTL depends on the tunnel model.
sections.plainLanguage: A router chooses the incoming countdown value, subtracts one and checks whether it remains above zero. The tunnel model determines which header supplies the value when a label is removed.

sections.title: The Uniform, Pipe and Short Pipe Models
sections.content:
In the Uniform model, the outer and inner TTL values are synchronized at tunnel entry and exit. Routers inside the LSP count toward the tunneled packet's TTL, so the tunnel is visible to nodes outside it.

In the Pipe model, the outer label TTL is configured separately from the tunneled TTL. The tunneled TTL is reduced at entry and exit, so it decreases by two across the LSP. The RFC specifies the Pipe model without PHP. The Short Pipe model uses the tunneled packet for forwarding treatment at egress and also reduces its TTL by two, with or without PHP.
sections.plainLanguage: The Uniform model makes the tunnel's routers count toward the packet's TTL. Pipe and Short Pipe keep an outer label countdown separate and reduce the tunneled packet's TTL at the two ends.

sections.title: Choosing and Updating TTL Values
sections.content:
When a router swaps a label, it sets the outgoing label TTL to oTTL. For a plain IP packet, it sets the outgoing IP TTL to oTTL. The RFC treats PHP separately because removing the last label exposes a different header.

For a Pipe-model pop, iTTL comes from the header exposed after the pop. For a Uniform-model pop, iTTL comes from the popped label. With a pushed Uniform label, the router copies the TTL from the header beneath it. With Pipe or Short Pipe labels, the router uses an operator-configured value, which is 255 by default in most implementations described by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: On a normal forwarding step, the router decreases the selected TTL by one. When it adds a label, it copies the inner value for Uniform or uses a configured value for Pipe models.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no security issues beyond those in RFC 3032 and RFC 3270. It defines no new protocol and does not expand an existing protocol.

The authors state that clarifying TTL handling can make troubleshooting simpler for providers and customers.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC clarifies how an existing packet counter changes. It does not add a new security mechanism or a new security issue.
